macroSectors.description: Covers businesses that make or trade basic materials sold largely on price and specification: chemicals and fertilisers, cement and building materials, metals and minerals, and paper, wood and jute. Their earnings move with input costs, global commodity prices, capacity cycles and demand from Indian construction, farming and manufacturing.

sectors.description: Makers of bulk, specialty and petroleum-based chemicals, industrial gases, explosives, inks, dyes and carbon black, plus fertilisers and crop-protection products. Profits depend on the spread between product prices and feedstock costs such as crude derivatives, natural gas and imported intermediates, and on export demand and competition from China.

Cement and other materials used to build homes, offices and infrastructure, such as roofing sheets, boards, blocks and facade systems. Demand follows housing, government infrastructure spending and the construction season, while fuel and freight are the main costs.

Producers of steel and ferro alloys, non-ferrous metals such as aluminium, copper and zinc, precious metals and mined minerals, along with metal and mineral traders. Earnings track global metal prices, raw material costs, the rupee and import competition, making this one of the most cyclical parts of the market.

Paper and paperboard makers, wood and other forest-product businesses, and jute mills. Their fortunes depend on fibre costs (wood, waste paper, raw jute), packaging and education demand, government buying of jute bags and imports from neighbouring countries.

industries.description: Companies that make bulk, specialty and petroleum-based chemicals, industrial gases, inks, dyes, carbon black and explosives, or trade in chemicals.
industries.businessOverview: Chemical makers convert feedstocks such as crude derivatives, natural gas, coal tar, salt and minerals into products used by almost every other industry. Bulk players compete mainly on cost and scale, while specialty players earn better margins from know-how, customer approvals and tailored products. Many Indian plants sell both at home and abroad, and pricing often moves with global supply, especially from China. Environmental clearances and pollution-control compliance are central to running a plant.
keyDemandDrivers: Downstream textiles, pharma, agrochemicals, autos and packaging

industries.description: Makers and marketers of fertilisers and crop-protection chemicals used by Indian and overseas farmers.
industries.businessOverview: Fertiliser companies produce or import urea, phosphatic and potassic nutrients and sell them to farmers at prices shaped by government subsidy schemes. Agrochemical companies make insecticides, herbicides and fungicides, either as branded products for Indian farmers or as technical-grade molecules for export. Both depend on the cropping season and the monsoon, and both carry heavy working capital through the year. Government policy on subsidies, product registrations and import duties shapes profitability.
keyRisks: Swings in imported input and gas prices

industries.description: Producers of cement and related products such as clinker and ready-mix concrete.
industries.businessOverview: Cement plants quarry limestone, burn it with fuel into clinker and grind it with gypsum, fly ash or slag into different cement types. Because cement is heavy and cheap per tonne, markets are regional and freight matters almost as much as production cost. Sales go through dealers to individual home builders and directly to developers and infrastructure contractors. Profit depends on regional demand, price discipline, fuel costs and how fully plants are used.
keyRisks: Capacity additions running ahead of demand
Coal, petcoke and diesel price spikes
Long monsoons or labour shortages slowing construction

industries.description: Makers and suppliers of building materials other than cement, such as roofing sheets, boards, blocks and facade systems.
industries.businessOverview: This group supplies materials that go into walls, roofs, ceilings and building exteriors. Products range from fibre-cement sheets and boards to aerated blocks, gypsum products and glass facade systems, and some firms run supply platforms for builders. Demand comes from homes, commercial buildings and rural construction, and many products compete with bricks, metal sheets and site-made plaster. Brands, dealer networks and project execution skills separate stronger players.
keyDemandDrivers: Commercial real estate and office build-out
Shift to faster, factory-made building materials
keyRisks: Input cost swings (cement, fibre, glass, aluminium)
Health and regulatory issues around certain materials

industries.description: Producers of iron, steel and the ferro alloys used to make steel.
industries.businessOverview: Ferrous metal companies turn iron ore, coal and other minerals into products ranging from sponge iron and pig iron to finished steel and alloys. Integrated plants run blast furnaces, often with captive raw materials, while secondary producers use electric or induction furnaces fed with sponge iron and scrap. Steel prices move with domestic demand, global prices and import flows, so margins swing widely. Raw material security and cost of production decide who comes through downturns in good shape.
keyDemandDrivers: Government capex on railways, roads and housing
Export demand and global steel prices
keyRisks: Coking coal and iron ore price swings

industries.description: Producers and refiners of aluminium, copper, zinc, lead and precious metals.
industries.businessOverview: Non-ferrous companies mine ores, smelt and refine metals, or recycle scrap, and sell them as ingots, rods, sheets and alloys. Prices are mostly set on global exchanges such as the London Metal Exchange, so earnings depend on global prices, the rupee and the cost of power and raw materials. Integrated miners with captive ore usually have lower costs than converters that buy concentrate or scrap. Demand comes from power, construction, autos, packaging, electricals and, for gold and silver, jewellery and investment.
keyDemandDrivers: Power grids, renewables and EV build-out
Jewellery and investment demand for gold and silver
keyRisks: Sharp falls in global metal prices

industries.description: Companies producing or recycling several different metals rather than one.
industries.businessOverview: Diversified metal companies run a mix of mining, smelting and recycling operations across metals such as zinc, lead, aluminium, copper, iron ore and silver, sometimes alongside oil, gas or power. A spread of metals can smooth earnings because metal prices do not always move together. Smaller players in this group recycle scrap, used batteries or residues into several metals. Group structure, debt and how cash moves between group entities can matter as much as the metal cycle.
keyDemandDrivers: Availability of scrap and recycling feedstock

industries.description: Miners and processors of industrial minerals such as iron ore, bauxite, bentonite, kaolin and calcium carbonate.
industries.businessOverview: Mining companies hold leases granted by state governments, extract ore or minerals and sell them raw, processed or upgraded. Some grind and purify minerals into fine grades used in paints, plastics, ceramics, drilling fluids and foundries. Earnings depend on volumes mined, realised prices and costs including royalty and other statutory payments. Lease tenure, environmental clearances and logistics to customers are key.
keyDemandDrivers: Paints, plastics, ceramics and paper output
keyRisks: Mining bans, environmental and court orders

industries.description: Traders and distributors of metals, scrap and minerals such as coal.
industries.businessOverview: Trading companies buy metals, scrap or minerals from producers or overseas suppliers and sell them to manufacturers, power plants and smaller buyers. They earn a margin per tonne plus income from services like credit, logistics, processing and sourcing. Margins are usually thin, so volume, inventory control and working-capital discipline drive returns. Price moves between purchase and sale can create gains or losses.
keyDemandDrivers: Import demand for coal and scrap
Fragmented buyers needing credit and small lots

industries.description: Makers of paper and paperboard, forest-based products and jute goods.
industries.businessOverview: Paper mills turn wood, agricultural residue or waste paper into writing paper, packaging board, newsprint and specialty grades. Forest-product businesses deal in timber, wood and other produce from forests and plantations. Jute mills spin raw jute into sacking, hessian and yarn, much of it bought by government agencies to pack food grains. All three depend on fibre costs, energy and environmental compliance, and face import competition.
keyDemandDrivers: Packaging demand from FMCG and e-commerce
keyRisks: Wood, waste paper and raw jute cost swings

basicIndustries.simplifiedExplanation: Companies that make basic chemicals in large volumes, such as acids, alkalis, solvents and intermediates. These are standard products, so buyers mostly choose on price and reliable supply.
basicIndustries.valueChainPosition: Upstream-to-midstream: buys salt, minerals, natural gas, coal and crude derivatives, and supplies other chemical makers plus textile, glass, detergent, paper, pharma and agrochemical industries.
basicIndustries.howTheyMakeMoney: They sell large volumes at prices close to domestic and import-parity levels. Profit is the spread between product price and feedstock plus energy cost, multiplied by how fully the plant runs.
revenueSources: Bulk chemical sales to industrial buyers
operatingCosts: Feedstock (salt, gas, benzene, propylene and similar)
Freight and handling of bulk liquids
basicIndustries.customersAndEndMarkets: Downstream chemical makers, textile processors, glass, soap and detergent makers, aluminium refiners, paper mills, pharma and water-treatment users.
basicIndustries.demandSupplyDrivers: Demand follows general industrial output. Supply is lumpy: a large new plant at home or abroad, or cheap Chinese and Middle Eastern exports, can pull prices down across the market.
basicIndustries.domesticInternationalExposure: Mostly sold in India but priced against imports; global prices of benzene, propylene, ammonia and similar feedstocks feed straight into costs.
basicIndustries.capexNote: Large continuous-process plants need heavy investment and scale to be cost-competitive.
basicIndustries.workingCapital: Moderate: feedstock and finished-goods stocks plus credit to industrial customers; price falls can hurt inventory values.
basicIndustries.regulation: Environmental clearance from MoEF and state pollution control boards, hazardous-chemical storage rules, and anti-dumping duties set on DGTR recommendations shape operations.
basicIndustries.competitiveAdvantages: Scale, feedstock integration, captive power and locations near customers or ports lower costs; costly plants and slow approvals keep new entrants few.

drivers.impact: Product and feedstock prices move with global chemical cycles and set the spread.
Cheap imports cap domestic prices; anti-dumping duties can restore them.
High fixed costs mean profits jump when plants run full and drop sharply when they do not.
Crude-linked feedstocks and fuel make up a large part of costs for many products.
Weak global demand pushes surplus product into India and lowers prices.

risks.detail: Global capacity additions can cause long stretches of low prices.
Accidents, breakdowns or pollution orders can halt output.
Power and fuel price spikes squeeze spreads quickly.
Lapse of anti-dumping protection can expose producers to imports.

basicIndustries.cyclicalityNote: Earnings swing with global chemical spreads and industrial demand.

basicIndustries.simplifiedExplanation: Companies that make chemicals designed for a specific job, such as an ingredient for a medicine, a crop-protection molecule or a coating additive. They sell on performance and quality, not just price.
basicIndustries.valueChainPosition: Midstream: buys basic and petrochemical inputs and supplies pharma, agrochemical, personal-care, paint, textile, construction and electronics makers in India and abroad.
basicIndustries.howTheyMakeMoney: They earn margins from process know-how, purity and reliability, often as an approved vendor or under multi-year supply agreements. Contract manufacturing for global innovators pays for dedicated capacity and technical skill.
basicIndustries.customersAndEndMarkets: Global and domestic pharma, agrochemical, personal-care, paint, textile, construction and electronics companies.
basicIndustries.demandSupplyDrivers: Demand depends on end-market growth and on global buyers shifting supply away from China. Customer destocking and Chinese price cuts can cause sharp temporary falls.
basicIndustries.domesticInternationalExposure: Many companies export a large part of output, so global demand, the rupee and Chinese competition matter a lot; several key inputs are imported.
basicIndustries.capexNote: Multipurpose plants need steady investment, plus spending on R&D, customer approvals and pollution control.
basicIndustries.workingCapital: Fairly high: export receivables, stocks of many raw materials and long customer qualification phases tie up cash.
basicIndustries.regulation: Pollution control board consents and environmental clearances, hazardous-chemical rules, and export-market rules such as EU REACH registration; customer audits act as a further check.
basicIndustries.competitiveAdvantages: Chemistry skills, long customer approval processes, safety and compliance records and backward integration make switching suppliers slow and costly.

drivers.impact: Orders from global pharma, agrochemical and consumer companies drive volumes.
Buyers diversifying away from China can bring new contracts to Indian makers.
Low-priced Chinese products pressure prices in India and export markets.
A weaker rupee lifts export realisations; a stronger rupee reduces them.
New molecules and greener chemistry open niches for skilled makers.

risks.detail: Global customers cutting inventory can reduce orders for several quarters.
A few large clients or molecules can dominate revenue.
Fires or leaks can halt production and invite regulatory action.
Aggressive pricing from Chinese producers can erode margins.

basicIndustries.cyclicalityNote: Steadier than bulk chemicals, but exposed to global inventory cycles and end-market slowdowns.

basicIndustries.simplifiedExplanation: Carbon black is a fine black powder made by burning heavy oil in a controlled way. It makes tyres and rubber stronger and gives black colour to inks, paints and plastics.
productsAndServices: Grades for belts, hoses and moulded rubber
Specialty grades for plastics, inks and coatings
Conductive carbon for batteries and cables
Co-generated power from process tail gas
basicIndustries.valueChainPosition: Midstream: buys carbon black feedstock oil from refineries and coal-tar distillers and supplies tyre makers, rubber goods makers and ink, paint and plastics compounders.
basicIndustries.howTheyMakeMoney: They sell by the tonne, usually under price formulas that pass feedstock changes to tyre customers with a lag. Specialty grades earn higher margins, and selling surplus power made from tail gas adds income.
basicIndustries.customersAndEndMarkets: Tyre makers are the largest buyers, followed by mechanical rubber goods, plastics masterbatch, ink, paint and battery makers.
basicIndustries.demandSupplyDrivers: Demand follows tyre production, which tracks new vehicle sales and replacement tyre demand. New plants and imports affect pricing.
basicIndustries.domesticInternationalExposure: Feedstock prices follow crude and coal-tar markets; Indian makers export to global tyre companies and face imports in turn.
basicIndustries.capexNote: Reactors, feedstock handling and co-generation plants are capital heavy.
basicIndustries.workingCapital: Moderate: feedstock is often imported in large lots and tyre customers get credit periods.
basicIndustries.regulation: State pollution control board consents and emission norms are important; anti-dumping duties on imported carbon black have been used in the past.
basicIndustries.competitiveAdvantages: Long approval cycles with tyre makers, scale, feedstock sourcing and a rising specialty mix protect established players.

drivers.impact: Feedstock cost moves with heavy oil and coal-tar prices.
Vehicle sales and replacement tyre demand set volumes.
Global tyre makers sourcing from India support export volumes.
Cheaper imports can pressure domestic prices.
Conductive carbon for batteries is a newer, higher-value market.

risks.detail: Fast feedstock price moves can hurt margins before contract prices reset.
Weak vehicle or tyre demand cuts volumes.
Tighter pollution rules can raise costs or restrict plants.
A small number of tyre makers buy most of the output.

basicIndustries.cyclicalityNote: Tied to auto and tyre cycles and crude-linked feedstock costs.

basicIndustries.simplifiedExplanation: Companies that make colours: dyes that colour fabric, yarn and leather, and pigments that colour paints, inks and plastics.
productsAndServices: Inorganic pigments such as ultramarine and iron oxide
basicIndustries.valueChainPosition: Midstream: buys benzene- and naphthalene-based intermediates and minerals, and supplies textile processors and paint, ink, plastics and detergent makers.
basicIndustries.howTheyMakeMoney: They sell colours by the kilogram, with margins tied to shade range, batch consistency and customer approvals. Backward integration into intermediates can widen margins.
revenueSources: Pigments for paint, ink and plastic makers
basicIndustries.customersAndEndMarkets: Textile dyeing and printing units serving garment makers and exporters, paint companies, ink makers, plastics compounders and detergent makers.
basicIndustries.demandSupplyDrivers: Textile and garment demand and paint and ink volumes drive sales. Pollution crackdowns in India or China can suddenly cut supply and lift prices.
basicIndustries.domesticInternationalExposure: Exports are significant and Chinese supply largely sets global prices; many intermediates are imported.
basicIndustries.capexNote: Batch plants are moderately costly, with significant spending on effluent treatment.
basicIndustries.workingCapital: High: many shades and grades must be stocked, and textile customers often take long credit.
basicIndustries.regulation: Close scrutiny of effluent by state pollution control boards and the National Green Tribunal; export markets restrict banned amines and heavy metals.
basicIndustries.competitiveAdvantages: Shade libraries, consistent quality, a clean compliance record and integration into intermediates protect established makers.

drivers.impact: Global textile and coatings demand sets export orders.
Chinese supply and pricing heavily influence realisations.
Pollution enforcement can shut capacity in India or abroad, changing supply.
Supply and price of aromatic intermediates drive costs.
Clothing and paint demand drives dye and pigment volumes.

risks.detail: Closure orders over effluent can halt plants.
Weak garment demand reduces dye offtake.
Low-cost imports can compress margins.
Small textile customers may delay payments.

basicIndustries.cyclicalityNote: Moves with textile and paint cycles and Chinese supply conditions.

basicIndustries.simplifiedExplanation: Companies that make industrial explosives and detonators used to break rock in mines and construction, and, in some cases, ammunition and propellants for defence.
productsAndServices: Propellants, warheads and ammunition for defence
basicIndustries.valueChainPosition: Midstream: buys ammonium nitrate and other chemicals and supplies coal, limestone and metal-ore miners, infrastructure contractors and the armed forces.
basicIndustries.howTheyMakeMoney: Mining explosives are sold through tenders and supply contracts, often with price-variation clauses linked to ammonium nitrate. Defence products are sold against orders from the Ministry of Defence and export customers, usually at higher margins.
revenueSources: Bulk explosives and blasting services for mines
basicIndustries.customersAndEndMarkets: Coal and metal miners, limestone quarries of cement makers, tunnel, road and dam builders, and defence buyers in India and abroad.
basicIndustries.demandSupplyDrivers: Demand follows mining output, especially coal, and tunnelling and quarrying for infrastructure. Defence demand depends on procurement orders and export approvals.
basicIndustries.domesticInternationalExposure: Mining demand is mostly domestic, with growing exports of industrial explosives and defence items; ammonium nitrate prices follow global markets.
basicIndustries.capexNote: Licensed plants and magazines need investment; defence facilities need more specialised spending.
basicIndustries.workingCapital: Moderate to high: tender customers can pay slowly and defence orders tie up inventory.
basicIndustries.regulation: Tightly licensed under the Explosives Act through PESO, with Ammonium Nitrate Rules on storage and handling; defence items need Ministry of Defence licences and export authorisation.
basicIndustries.competitiveAdvantages: Licences, safety records, on-site blasting know-how and defence qualifications make entry difficult.

drivers.impact: Roads, tunnels, dams and railways raise blasting needs.
Coal production is the largest user of bulk explosives.
Ammunition and propellant orders add higher-margin revenue.
Ammonium nitrate cost changes flow into margins until contract prices reset.
Overseas mining and defence orders widen the market.

risks.detail: An accident can stop plants and trigger licence reviews.
Competitive tenders from large miners can keep margins thin.
Defence orders are lumpy and can slip.
Ammonium nitrate price spikes squeeze margins.

basicIndustries.cyclicalityNote: Mining demand is fairly steady, while defence orders follow government budgets.

basicIndustries.simplifiedExplanation: Companies that turn oil- and gas-based feedstocks into plastics, synthetic rubber and chemical building blocks used to make thousands of everyday products.
basicIndustries.valueChainPosition: Midstream: buys naphtha, natural gas, ethylene, propylene or aromatics from refineries and crackers, and supplies plastics processors and polyester, detergent, packaging and auto-part makers.
basicIndustries.howTheyMakeMoney: They earn the spread between polymer or chemical prices and feedstock cost, which tracks Asian benchmark prices. Running large plants at high utilisation is key.
basicIndustries.customersAndEndMarkets: Plastics processors, packaging converters, polyester and textile makers, detergent makers, and pipe, appliance and auto-part manufacturers.
basicIndustries.demandSupplyDrivers: Demand tracks packaging, construction, consumer goods and autos. Large new crackers in China and the Middle East can depress global spreads for long periods.
basicIndustries.domesticInternationalExposure: India imports a good part of its polymer needs, so domestic prices follow import parity; feedstock prices follow crude and global gas.
basicIndustries.capexNote: Crackers and polymer plants are among the most capital-intensive projects in industry.
basicIndustries.workingCapital: Moderate: feedstock and product stocks carry price risk, while distributors carry much of the credit to small processors.
basicIndustries.regulation: Environmental clearance and pollution norms, BIS quality control orders on several polymers and chemicals, and anti-dumping or safeguard duties via DGTR affect imports.
basicIndustries.competitiveAdvantages: Feedstock integration with refineries, scale and nearness to customers give cost leadership; smaller players survive in niche grades.

drivers.impact: Naphtha and other feedstocks move with crude, shifting costs.
Global polymer and chemical spreads decide profitability.
Import parity and trade duties set domestic prices.
Packaging, appliances and autos drive polymer use.
Global capacity additions versus demand shape the cycle.

risks.detail: New capacity abroad can depress spreads for years.
Sudden crude moves can squeeze margins.
Bans on single-use plastics can reduce some end uses.
Unplanned shutdowns hit volumes and fixed-cost absorption.

basicIndustries.cyclicalityNote: Spreads follow global petrochemical capacity cycles and crude prices.

basicIndustries.simplifiedExplanation: Companies that make the inks used to print packaging, newspapers, magazines and labels.
productsAndServices: Gravure and flexo inks for flexible packaging
Offset inks for publications and commercial print
basicIndustries.valueChainPosition: Midstream: buys pigments, resins, solvents and additives, and supplies packaging converters, printing presses and newspaper publishers.
basicIndustries.howTheyMakeMoney: They sell formulated inks with colour matching and on-press technical support, often as approved suppliers to packaging converters. Margins depend on the gap between selling prices and petroleum-based raw material costs.
basicIndustries.customersAndEndMarkets: Flexible packaging converters serving food and FMCG brands, carton makers, commercial printers and newspaper publishers.
basicIndustries.demandSupplyDrivers: Packaged food and FMCG volumes drive packaging inks, while newspaper and magazine circulation trends drive publication inks.
basicIndustries.domesticInternationalExposure: Sales are mainly domestic; key pigments, resins and solvents follow global petrochemical prices and some are imported.
basicIndustries.capexNote: Mixing and milling plants need modest investment relative to sales.
basicIndustries.workingCapital: Moderate: many colours and grades in stock, plus credit to converters and printers.
basicIndustries.regulation: Pollution control consents for solvent handling; food-packaging inks are expected to meet BIS standards referenced in FSSAI packaging rules.
basicIndustries.competitiveAdvantages: Colour-matching capability, technical service at the press, approvals with large brand owners and access to global technology.

drivers.impact: Packaged food and FMCG sales drive packaging print volumes.
Solvents and resins track crude, moving costs.
Digital printing and shrinking print media change the product mix.
Food-safety norms push demand toward safer, premium inks.

risks.detail: Falling newspaper use reduces publication-ink demand.
Pigment and solvent price rises can run ahead of selling-price hikes.
Large converters negotiate hard on price.

basicIndustries.cyclicalityNote: Packaging demand is steady, but margins swing with petrochemical input costs.

basicIndustries.simplifiedExplanation: Companies that buy chemicals from manufacturers or overseas suppliers and resell them to smaller industrial users. They are distributors, not manufacturers.
basicIndustries.valueChainPosition: Midstream distribution: sits between chemical producers or importers and small and mid-sized manufacturers who buy in smaller lots.
basicIndustries.howTheyMakeMoney: They earn a trading margin or commission on each lot sold, plus value from the storage, credit and logistics they offer buyers.
basicIndustries.customersAndEndMarkets: Small and mid-sized makers of paints, textiles, pharma, agrochemicals, plastics and cleaning products.
basicIndustries.demandSupplyDrivers: Volumes follow activity among small manufacturers; price swings between buying and selling change profits.
basicIndustries.domesticInternationalExposure: Many traders import their products, so currency moves, freight and global chemical prices matter.
basicIndustries.capexNote: Assets are mainly warehouses, tanks and vehicles.
basicIndustries.workingCapital: High: inventory and customer credit are the core of the business, funded mostly by bank lines.
basicIndustries.regulation: Hazardous-chemical storage and transport rules, GST and customs compliance; some chemicals need special licences.
basicIndustries.competitiveAdvantages: Supplier agency rights, storage near industrial clusters, credit-assessment skill and customer relationships.

drivers.impact: Rising prices give inventory gains; falling prices cause losses.
A weaker rupee raises the cost of imported products.
Access to bank credit limits how much stock and customer credit a trader can carry.
Downstream manufacturing activity sets volumes.

risks.detail: Sharp price falls hurt stock bought at higher prices.
Small buyers may default or pay late.
Suppliers can switch distributors or sell directly.

basicIndustries.cyclicalityNote: Volumes and margins follow chemical price cycles and small-industry demand.

basicIndustries.simplifiedExplanation: Companies that separate air into oxygen, nitrogen and argon, or make gases such as hydrogen, carbon dioxide and refrigerants, and supply them to factories and hospitals.
productsAndServices: On-site gas plants and steam supply
basicIndustries.valueChainPosition: Midstream: uses air, electricity and chemical feedstock to produce gases and supplies steel, chemicals, refining, glass, electronics, healthcare and food industries.
basicIndustries.howTheyMakeMoney: Large customers such as steel plants get gas from on-site plants under long-term take-or-pay contracts, giving steady income. Smaller customers buy liquid gas by tanker or cylinder at higher prices, and medical and specialty gases earn premium margins.
revenueSources: Medical gases and hospital pipeline systems
basicIndustries.customersAndEndMarkets: Steel plants, refineries, chemical and glass makers, electronics and solar units, hospitals, food and beverage companies and metal fabricators.
basicIndustries.demandSupplyDrivers: Steel and industrial output drive bulk volumes, while hospital and specialty uses grow more steadily; merchant prices depend on local surplus capacity.
basicIndustries.domesticInternationalExposure: Mostly domestic because gases are costly to transport; some specialty gases and refrigerants are imported or exported.
basicIndustries.capexNote: Air separation units, cylinders and tanker fleets need heavy upfront investment.
basicIndustries.workingCapital: Low to moderate: contracts bill monthly, though hospital and government dues can be slow.
basicIndustries.regulation: Cylinders, tankers and storage are regulated by PESO; medical oxygen falls under drug rules and can face price controls; refrigerants face phase-down rules under the Montreal Protocol.
basicIndustries.competitiveAdvantages: Long-term contracts, plants located at customer sites, dense distribution and safety know-how create high entry barriers.

drivers.impact: Electricity is the largest cost of air separation, so tariff changes move margins.
Steel and industrial output decide how fully gas plants run.
Hospital growth drives medical oxygen and gas systems.
Electronics, solar and green hydrogen projects create new gas demand.
Price caps on medical oxygen and refrigerant phase-downs affect earnings.

risks.detail: A steel plant cutting output reduces on-site volumes.
Surplus liquid gas can drive down spot prices.
Cylinder or plant accidents bring regulatory action.
Higher tariffs hurt margins where contracts lack pass-through.

basicIndustries.cyclicalityNote: Contracted on-site supply is steady, while merchant volumes follow industrial cycles.

basicIndustries.simplifiedExplanation: Companies that make or import plant nutrients such as urea, DAP and complex fertilisers and sell them to farmers, mostly at prices shaped by government subsidies.
basicIndustries.valueChainPosition: Upstream-to-downstream: buys natural gas, rock phosphate, phosphoric acid, ammonia and potash (much of it imported) and sells through dealers and cooperatives to farmers.
basicIndustries.howTheyMakeMoney: Urea sells at a government-fixed farm price and the maker receives a subsidy covering the gap to its normative cost, so beating efficiency norms drives profit. Phosphatic and potassic fertilisers get a fixed subsidy per nutrient under the Nutrient Based Subsidy scheme, so margins depend on global raw material prices and the selling price companies can charge.
operatingCosts: Phosphoric acid, rock phosphate and ammonia
basicIndustries.customersAndEndMarkets: Farmers across India, reached through dealers, cooperatives and state marketing federations; some industrial buyers for chemicals.
basicIndustries.demandSupplyDrivers: Demand depends on the monsoon, cropped area and crop mix, and on the farm price after subsidy. Supply depends on global raw material availability and government import planning.
basicIndustries.domesticInternationalExposure: India relies heavily on imported gas, phosphates and potash, so global prices and the rupee matter, while sales are almost entirely domestic.
basicIndustries.capexNote: Urea, ammonia and phosphoric acid plants are large and energy- or acid-intensive.
basicIndustries.workingCapital: High and seasonal: subsidy dues from the government and stocking ahead of kharif and rabi seasons tie up cash.
basicIndustries.regulation: Heavily controlled by the Department of Fertilizers through urea pricing policy, the Nutrient Based Subsidy scheme and movement plans; quality is governed by the Fertiliser Control Order.
basicIndustries.competitiveAdvantages: Energy-efficient plants, raw material tie-ups abroad, strong dealer networks and brand recall among farmers.

drivers.impact: Subsidy rates, urea pricing norms and import decisions directly set profits.
Rainfall and sown area drive fertiliser offtake each season.
Global prices of gas, ammonia, phosphates and potash move costs.
A weaker rupee raises the cost of imported inputs.
Delayed subsidies are funded with borrowing, so rates affect costs.

risks.detail: Late government payments raise debt and interest costs.
Lower nutrient subsidies can squeeze phosphatic margins.
Global supply disruptions can spike input costs.
Weak rains reduce demand and leave stock unsold.

basicIndustries.cyclicalityNote: Farm demand is steady, but margins depend on subsidy policy and global input prices.

basicIndustries.simplifiedExplanation: Companies that make chemicals protecting crops from insects, weeds and diseases, sold as branded products to farmers or as bulk ingredients to global agrochemical companies.
basicIndustries.valueChainPosition: Midstream-to-downstream: buys chemical intermediates (many from China) to make technical-grade molecules, which are formulated and sold through distributors and retailers to farmers, or exported.
basicIndustries.howTheyMakeMoney: Branded domestic sellers earn from distribution reach and farmer trust; generic exporters earn from low-cost manufacturing and product registrations in many countries; contract makers earn from producing patented molecules for innovators.
basicIndustries.customersAndEndMarkets: Indian farmers through dealers and retailers, global agrochemical companies, and distributors in the Americas, Europe, Africa and Asia.
basicIndustries.demandSupplyDrivers: Pest pressure, rainfall and crop prices drive farmer demand; global channel inventory and Chinese pricing drive export demand.
basicIndustries.domesticInternationalExposure: Many companies are strongly export-oriented; reliance on Chinese intermediates and global pricing makes them sensitive to China and the rupee.
basicIndustries.capexNote: Multipurpose chemical plants and formulation units need steady investment and pollution-control spending.
basicIndustries.workingCapital: High and seasonal: stock is built before kharif and rabi, dealers get long credit and export receivables are large.
basicIndustries.regulation: Products must be registered with the Central Insecticides Board and Registration Committee under the Insecticides Act; molecule bans and export-market registrations (such as US EPA and EU rules) shape portfolios.
basicIndustries.competitiveAdvantages: Product registrations, distribution reach, brand trust among farmers, low-cost chemistry and long relationships with global innovators.

drivers.impact: Rains, pest incidence and crop area decide domestic sales each season.
Global farm demand and channel inventory drive export orders.
Chinese technical prices set the floor for generic molecules.
Registrations and bans change which products can be sold.
Moves export realisations and imported input costs.

risks.detail: Excess stock with distributors can cut orders sharply.
Drought or floods reduce pesticide use.
Bans in India or abroad can wipe out product lines.
Supply or price shocks in Chinese intermediates hurt costs.

basicIndustries.cyclicalityNote: Crop protection is a farm necessity, but export cycles and weather cause sharp swings.

basicIndustries.simplifiedExplanation: Companies that make cement, the grey powder that binds concrete, and related products like ready-mix concrete. Plants sit near limestone mines and sell mostly within their region.
productsAndServices: Portland Pozzolana Cement (PPC) and slag cement
basicIndustries.valueChainPosition: Upstream-to-midstream: mines limestone and buys coal, petcoke, gypsum, fly ash and slag, then sells through dealers to home builders and directly to developers and infrastructure contractors.
basicIndustries.howTheyMakeMoney: They earn the price per tonne minus the cost of fuel, power, raw materials and freight. Selling through dealers to individual home builders (trade sales) usually fetches better prices than bulk project sales.
revenueSources: Non-trade sales to developers and infrastructure projects
operatingCosts: Limestone, fly ash, slag and gypsum
basicIndustries.customersAndEndMarkets: Individual home builders, real estate developers, road, rail, metro and irrigation contractors, and industrial and commercial construction.
basicIndustries.demandSupplyDrivers: Demand follows housing, infrastructure and commercial construction and slows during the monsoon. Large capacity additions in a region can hurt prices until demand catches up.
basicIndustries.domesticInternationalExposure: Almost fully domestic; imported coal and petcoke prices and the rupee affect fuel costs.
basicIndustries.capexNote: Integrated plants, limestone mines, captive power and logistics require heavy investment per tonne of capacity.
basicIndustries.workingCapital: Low: dealer sales are largely on short credit or advance, with some fuel and clinker inventory.
basicIndustries.regulation: Limestone leases are auctioned under the MMDR Act, cement needs BIS certification, environmental clearance and emission norms apply, and the CCI watches pricing conduct.
basicIndustries.competitiveAdvantages: Limestone reserves, plants close to markets, low-cost fuel and power, brand pull with dealers and efficient logistics.

drivers.impact: Government spending on roads, rail and housing boosts volumes.
Housing and commercial construction drive dealer and project demand.
Coal, petcoke and diesel costs move cost per tonne.
Regional supply additions versus demand decide pricing power.
Rains pause construction; good harvests support rural housing.

risks.detail: Fresh capacity in a region can trigger price cuts.
Costlier coal and petcoke squeeze margins.
Weak housing or delayed government projects reduce volumes.
Mining, environmental or competition rulings can affect operations.

basicIndustries.cyclicalityNote: Volumes and prices follow construction activity and regional capacity cycles.

basicIndustries.simplifiedExplanation: Companies that make or supply building materials other than cement, such as roofing sheets, boards, blocks, panels and glass facades.
productsAndServices: Wall panels and prefabricated building systems
basicIndustries.valueChainPosition: Midstream: buys cement, fly ash, fibre, gypsum, glass and aluminium, and supplies dealers, developers, contractors and facade projects.
basicIndustries.howTheyMakeMoney: Product makers sell through dealers or directly to projects, earning margins from brands, reach and a lower installed cost than traditional methods. Facade and supply-platform firms earn on project contracts or trading margins.
revenueSources: Dealer sales of sheets, boards and blocks
operatingCosts: Cement, fly ash, fibre and gypsum
basicIndustries.customersAndEndMarkets: Rural and semi-urban households (roofing), real estate developers, commercial and office buildings, warehouses and infrastructure contractors.
basicIndustries.demandSupplyDrivers: Housing, rural incomes and commercial construction drive demand, helped by a shift from site-made bricks and plaster to factory-made products.
basicIndustries.domesticInternationalExposure: Mostly domestic; inputs such as fibre, gypsum and glass are partly imported or priced globally.
basicIndustries.capexNote: Plants are moderately capital-intensive, while project and trading businesses need little fixed capital.
basicIndustries.workingCapital: Moderate to high: dealer stocks and project receivables, with retention money held back on facade contracts.
basicIndustries.regulation: BIS standards for building products and environmental norms; asbestos-based products face health and regulatory scrutiny.
basicIndustries.competitiveAdvantages: Brand, dealer reach in rural markets, plants near fly-ash sources and design and execution skill for facades.

drivers.impact: Residential and commercial construction drive product demand.
Farm incomes affect demand for roofing sheets and low-cost building products.
Public projects and warehouses add volume.
Cement, fibre, glass and aluminium costs move margins.
Prefabricated and lighter materials replace bricks and plaster.

risks.detail: Local makers compete hard on price.
Raw material spikes are hard to pass on quickly.
Facade and supply contracts suffer when developers slow down.
Curbs on asbestos or other materials could hit product lines.

basicIndustries.cyclicalityNote: Demand rises and falls with housing and commercial construction.
